name: Gas injection and WAG (hydrocarbon, CO2, nitrogen)
aliases: Gas injection and WAG (hydrocarbon, CO2, nitrogen)
principle: Gas (natural gas, nitrogen or CO2) is injected to maintain pressure or become miscible with oil; water-alternating-gas (WAG) cycles gas and water to improve sweep. Gas injection projects made up 56% of the 374 EOR projects counted worldwide in 2017 (CO2 44%, other gas 12%).

process_steps.name: Inject gas or alternate gas and water

performance.metric: share of 2017 EOR projects using CO2

source.note: Wikipedia, Enhanced oil recovery, read 25 October 2026 (secondary source)

performance.basis: depth threshold for miscible CO2 flooding as stated in the source

source.note: Wikipedia, Enhanced oil recovery, read 25 October 2026 (secondary source)

performance.basis: WAG pilots typically yield 5-10% of OOIP incremental recovery, with up to 20% in a few pilots.

source.note: Belazreg & Mahmood, WAG pilot review (2020), read 2026-11-17

advantages: CO2 can be stored while producing oil
limitations: WAG-specific results not available: ScienceDirect review blocked

reference_plants.name: Statfjord WAG (water-alternating-gas injection)
reference_plants.capacity: largest oil field in the North Sea at start-up (production began 23 Nov 1979); injection converted from water-only to WAG in the late 1990s

source.note: Equinor news, 17 Mar 2003: "Statfjord's injection system was converted in the late 1990s from water alone to water alternating gas (WAG)". Field facts from norskpetroleum.no/en/facts/field/statfjord (start-up 1979, WAG pressure support, depressurisation from 2007); both read 2026-10-28

notes: Process provenance: Documents immiscible WAG core-flood experiments - alternating water and nitrogen gas slugs injected in cycles, with a reported design of 0.3 PV total injected water plus gas per cycle at a 2:1 gas/water ratio, and pore-scale visualisation of the displacement.
